prompt: When reading the volume of a liquid in a graduated measuring cylinder, an observer consistently views the bottom of the curved meniscus from above the horizontal line of sight. What type of error does this introduce?
options: A random error that causes readings to scatter unpredictably above and below the true volume.
A systematic error that causes all volume readings to be consistently lower than the true volume.
A systematic error that causes all volume readings to be consistently higher than the true volume.
No error, because liquid surfaces are always flat across the graduation markings.

answer.explanation: Viewing from above projects the meniscus onto a graduation higher up on the scale. Since this is done consistently, it introduces a systematic error that makes all readings too high.

distractor_explanations: Consistent viewing from one fixed angle produces a systematic offset, not random scatter.
Viewing from above projects the line of sight downward across the cylinder, aligning the meniscus with a higher mark, not lower.
Correct. Parallax from viewing from above consistently projects the meniscus against higher scale divisions.
Liquids form curved meniscuses, and parallax occurs whenever the line of sight is oblique.
hints: Draw a mental ray from the eye through the meniscus to the scale markings on the wall of the cylinder.
If your eye is above the meniscus, does the line of sight hit the scale above or below the meniscus level?
solution: A systematic error that causes all readings to be consistently higher than the true volume.
teacher_walkthrough: Parallax from an eye positioned above the meniscus causes the line of sight to slope downwards.
When looking down at the front scale, the line intersects a division higher than the true liquid level.
Because this angle is maintained consistently for all readings, it is a systematic positive error.

provenance.independence_statement: Authored to test physical origin and direction of parallax systematic error.
